answers.answer: A reranker works inside the list the first pass already returned, holding the documents selected so far and picking the next one from those not yet selected. It changes the order, and once the list is cut to a context budget it changes which passages survive. It cannot introduce a document that retrieval never returned, so a recall failure passes through it unchanged.
accept: reranking only reorders or selects within the already retrieved list
it cannot add a document the first pass never returned, so the recall failure remains
what it does change is order, and membership once the list is truncated

answers.answer: Marginal relevance combines relevance to the query with a novelty term computed against the documents already selected, so a candidate's score depends on the set built so far and not on the query alone. That makes selection incremental: pick the best candidate, move it into the selected set, then rescore the remaining candidates, because what counts as novel has changed.
accept: the score contains a term measuring similarity to the documents already selected
the score therefore depends on the set chosen so far, not on the query alone
selection has to be incremental or greedy, rescoring the remaining candidates after each pick

answers.answer: At lambda equals 1 it computes the standard relevance-ranked list, and at lambda equals 0 the paper says it computes a maximal diversity ranking among the documents already retrieved. Intermediate values optimise a linear combination of the two criteria. A learner who also notes that the equation as printed in the paper collapses to zero for every candidate at lambda equals 0, so the printed form does not reproduce the second endpoint, has read the chapter closely.
accept: lambda equals 1 gives the standard relevance ranking
lambda equals 0 gives a maximal diversity ranking among the retrieved documents
values in between optimise a linear combination of relevance and novelty

answers.answer: The criterion penalises a candidate for resembling passages already chosen, so the near-duplicates below the first one are demoted and the set spreads across more of what the query could have meant, which matters because near-identical passages spend several context slots on one fact. What you give up is that the lower slots are no longer the closest matches to the query: a passage can be pushed down purely for being similar to one already selected.
accept: duplicates or near-duplicates are demoted because the score penalises similarity to what is already selected
the set covers more of the query's possible readings, or wastes fewer context slots on one repeated fact
the cost is that lower positions are no longer the highest query-similarity passages, since novelty is traded against relevance

answers.answer: He has merged a ranking metric with an answer metric. nDCG and diversity scores are computed from the retrieved passages and their embeddings before the model runs; answer quality is computed from what the model wrote. The chapter gives two cases where they separate: ARAGOG reports Sentence Window Retrieval with high retrieval precision and lower answer similarity, and in Dartboard's integrated column the Oracle row has the highest nDCG at .826 with 36 percent QA while D-CC has .595 nDCG and 42 percent QA.
accept: distinguishes a ranking or retrieval metric, computed from the retrieved set before generation, from an answer metric computed from the model's output
notes that a gain in one does not imply a gain in the other
names a concrete case: ARAGOG's Sentence Window Retrieval, or the Dartboard integrated column where the highest nDCG row is not the highest QA row

answers.answer: It answers how well each method can do on that benchmark when its parameter is tuned, which is the fair question for comparing algorithms. It does not tell you how a method behaves away from that optimum, and the optimum was found by scoring the sweep against the benchmark's own correct answers, which you do not have for your corpus. The number is the ceiling of a tuned method, not the score you get from a parameter you guessed.
accept: the table compares methods at their best tuned parameter on that benchmark
it says nothing about behaviour at other parameter values, or about the value you would pick without a sweep
the sweep is scored using the benchmark's labels or correct answers, which a new corpus does not come with

answers.answer: The limitation ARAGOG names is that its findings rest on a single dataset of 107 questions, and the way to test that is a different dataset. REBEL takes its setup and that same 107 question dataset from ARAGOG's repository, so on the axis in question the two are one corpus reported twice rather than two independent results. REBEL adds a different method and a different emphasis; it does not add dataset independence.
accept: the shared dataset and setup mean the second study does not test generalisation to a different dataset
agreement between them is one corpus measured twice on that axis, not independent replication
answering ARAGOG's stated limitation requires a different dataset, which REBEL does not supply

answers.answer: No source cited in the chapter measures the diversity parameter against answer quality across its range. The closest is a Dartboard figure caption plotting end-to-end QA as the diversity parameter varies, with no values given in the text, and everything else reports a single best-of-sweep point. The 1998 null result is about summarization sentence precision at three lambda values, not about answer quality. So the correct statement is that these sources do not establish the relationship, which is an absence of measurement rather than a measured absence of effect.
accept: the cited sources do not report the parameter measured against answer quality across its range, only best-of-sweep points and one figure caption with no values
states the gap as a fact about these sources rather than about the whole literature
distinguishes no measurement from a measured null, and notes the 1998 null was on summarization precision, not answer quality
